questions.q: Which of these compounds is a 2-amino acid?
questions.solution: In a 2-amino acid the amine group is on carbon 2, the carbon next to the COOH group. \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH(CH_{3})COOH}\) (alanine) fits. \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH_{2}CH_{2}COOH}\) is 3-aminopropanoic acid, with the amine on carbon 3; the others have no carboxylic acid group.

questions.q: Which is the zwitterion of glycine, \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH_{2}COOH}\)?
questions.solution: A zwitterion carries a positive and a negative charge on the same molecule but is neutral overall. The COOH group donates \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) to the \(\mathrm{NH_{2}}\) group, giving \(\mathrm{H_{3}N^{+}CH_{2}COO^{-}}\). \(\mathrm{H_{3}N^{+}CH_{2}COOH}\) is the ion in acid, and \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH_{2}COO^{-}}\) the ion in alkali.

questions.q: Alanine, shown, is dissolved in a solution of low pH. Which species is mainly present?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of alanine: a carbon carrying an NH2 group, a CH3 group and a COOH group.

questions.solution: In acid there is a high concentration of \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\), so the \(\mathrm{COO^{-}}\) of the zwitterion is protonated while the amine stays as \(\mathrm{NH_{3}^{+}}\): the ion is \(\mathrm{H_{3}N^{+}CH(CH_{3})COOH}\), with an overall positive charge. (A common slip is to protonate only the amine and leave \(\mathrm{COO^{-}}\), which is the zwitterion.)

questions.q: Alanine is dissolved in aqueous sodium hydroxide. Which species is mainly present?
questions.solution: Hydroxide ions remove \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) from the \(\mathrm{NH_{3}^{+}}\) group of the zwitterion, so in alkali the amino acid is \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH(CH_{3})COO^{-}}\), with an overall negative charge. The carboxylate group stays ionised.

questions.q: Why do amino acids such as glycine have high melting points, for molecules of their size?

options.A: They have strong covalent bonds between the molecules.
options.B: In the solid they exist as zwitterions, held together by strong ionic attractions between the charged groups of neighbouring ions.
options.C: They form long polymer chains in the solid.
options.D: They have permanent dipole–dipole forces between the C=O groups only.

questions.solution: Solid amino acids are made of zwitterions such as \(\mathrm{H_{3}N^{+}CH_{2}COO^{-}}\). The \(\mathrm{NH_{3}^{+}}\) of one ion is strongly attracted to the \(\mathrm{COO^{-}}\) of its neighbours, as in an ionic lattice, so a lot of energy is needed to melt them. The same charges make them soluble in water.

questions.q: An aqueous solution of naturally occurring alanine rotates the plane of plane-polarised light, but a solution of glycine does not. Why?

options.A: Glycine is a zwitterion in solution, but alanine is not.
options.B: Glycine molecules are too small to interact with light.
options.C: The 2-carbon of glycine carries two hydrogen atoms, so glycine has no chiral centre; the 2-carbon of alanine has four different groups.
options.D: Glycine is a racemic mixture of two enantiomers.

questions.solution: Optical activity needs a chiral carbon, with four different groups. In alanine the 2-carbon carries H, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\), \(\mathrm{NH_{2}}\) and COOH, and natural alanine is a single enantiomer. In glycine the 2-carbon has two H atoms, so the molecule is identical to its mirror image and has no enantiomers. Both are zwitterions in solution.

questions.q: One molecule of glycine and one molecule of alanine react to form a dipeptide. How many different dipeptides are possible?
questions.solution: Either amino acid can provide the COOH group that forms the peptide link: glycine's COOH with alanine's \(\mathrm{NH_{2}}\) gives Gly–Ala, and alanine's COOH with glycine's \(\mathrm{NH_{2}}\) gives Ala–Gly. These are different molecules (structural isomers). (Counting only one way round is a common slip.) So the number of dipeptides is 2.

questions.q: The tripeptide shown is completely hydrolysed. Which amino acids are formed?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a tripeptide: three units joined by two C(=O)–NH links; the first unit has no side group, the second a CH3 side group, and the third a CH2OH side group and a COOH end.

questions.solution: Hydrolysis breaks each peptide link, C(=O)–NH, adding OH to the C=O and H to the N. Reading along the chain: \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH_{2}COOH}\) (glycine, R = H), \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH(CH_{3})COOH}\) (alanine, R = \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\)) and \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH(CH_{2}OH)COOH}\) (serine, R = \(\mathrm{CH_{2}OH}\)). Cysteine has \(\mathrm{CH_{2}SH}\), not \(\mathrm{CH_{2}OH}\).

questions.q: Which conditions are used to hydrolyse a protein into its amino acids in the laboratory?

options.A: Dilute sodium hydroxide at room temperature for a few minutes
options.D: Hydrochloric acid of about 6 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\), heated under reflux for several hours

questions.solution: Peptide links are strong, so hydrolysis needs concentrated acid (about 6 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) hydrochloric acid) and heating under reflux for several hours (around 24 hours). In the body, enzymes do the same job at body temperature.

questions.q: A protein hydrolysate is analysed by thin-layer chromatography. One spot moves 4.5 cm from the baseline while the solvent front moves 7.5 cm. In this solvent the \(R_{\text{f}}\) values are: glycine 0.26, alanine 0.38, valine 0.60, leucine 0.73. Which amino acid is the spot?
questions.solution: \(R_{\text{f}} = \frac{\text{distance moved by spot}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}} = \frac{4.5}{7.5} = 0.60\), which matches valine. (A common slip is to measure the spot from the solvent front, \(\frac{3.0}{7.5} = 0.40\), which points to alanine.)

questions.q: Amino acids are colourless. How are their spots located on a thin-layer chromatogram?

options.A: By spraying with ninhydrin solution and warming, or by shining ultraviolet light on the plate
options.B: By adding bromine water to the plate
options.C: By measuring the boiling point of each spot
options.D: By heating the plate until the spots char black

questions.solution: Ninhydrin reacts with amino acids to give purple spots once the plate is warmed. Alternatively, a plate containing a fluorescent dye glows under ultraviolet light except where a spot absorbs it, so the spots show up dark. Their positions are then marked and the Rf values measured.

questions.q: Which bonds maintain the α-helix of the secondary structure of a protein?

options.A: Covalent bonds between the side chains of neighbouring amino acids
options.B: Ionic bonds between the NH3+ and COO− groups at the ends of the chain
options.D: Hydrogen bonds between the N–H of one peptide link and the C=O of another peptide link further along the chain

questions.solution: The secondary structure (α-helix or β-pleated sheet) is held by hydrogen bonds between the δ+ hydrogen of an N–H group and a lone pair on the δ− oxygen of a C=O group in another peptide link. Sulfur–sulfur bonds and interactions between side chains hold the tertiary structure.

questions.q: Two cysteine residues in a protein chain, each with the side chain \(\mathrm{-CH_{2}SH}\), help to hold its tertiary structure. Which bond forms between them?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of cysteine: a carbon carrying NH2, COOH and a CH2SH side chain.

options.A: A hydrogen bond between the two SH groups
options.B: A covalent sulfur–sulfur bond (a disulfide bridge)
options.C: An ionic bond between the two sulfur atoms
options.D: A peptide link between the two side chains

questions.solution: The two thiol groups are oxidised, each losing a hydrogen atom, and a covalent S–S bond forms: \(\mathrm{-CH_{2}SH + HSCH_{2}- \rightarrow -CH_{2}S{-}SCH_{2}- + 2[H]}\). This disulfide bridge can join distant parts of the chain, fixing the folded shape.

questions.q: An enzyme catalyses a reaction of only one enantiomer of its substrate. Which is the best explanation?

options.A: The other enantiomer has a different molecular formula, so it cannot fit.
options.B: The other enantiomer rotates plane-polarised light, which deactivates the enzyme.
options.C: The active site is stereospecific: its groups are arranged in 3D so that only one enantiomer can bind to all of them at the same time.
options.D: Enzymes can only bind molecules that are achiral.

questions.solution: The active site is a 3D pocket whose groups form bonds (for example hydrogen bonds and ionic attractions) with particular groups on the substrate. Enantiomers have the same groups arranged differently in space, so only one of them lines up with all the binding sites at once. Enantiomers have identical molecular formulae.

questions.q: What is a nucleotide made of?

options.A: A phosphate group, the sugar 2-deoxyribose and one of four bases
options.B: A phosphate group, an amino acid and one of four bases
options.C: Two bases joined by hydrogen bonds
options.D: A sugar and a base joined by a peptide link

questions.solution: A DNA nucleotide is a phosphate group bonded to 2-deoxyribose, which is bonded to one of the bases adenine, cytosine, guanine or thymine. Nucleotides join through phosphate–sugar bonds to make a single strand.

questions.q: One strand of DNA has the base sequence A T G C C A. What is the sequence of bases on the complementary strand, in the same order?

options.A: A T G C C A
options.B: A C G T T A
options.C: G C A T T G
options.D: T A C G G T

questions.solution: Adenine pairs with thymine, and guanine pairs with cytosine. Each base is replaced by its partner: A→T, T→A, G→C, C→G, C→G, A→T, giving T A C G G T.

questions.q: The base shown is guanine. Which base does it pair with in DNA, and how many hydrogen bonds form in the pair?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a DNA base: a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring, carrying an NH2 group and a C=O group, with N–H groups in the rings.

questions.solution: Guanine pairs with cytosine, forming three hydrogen bonds; adenine pairs with thymine, forming two. The shapes and positions of the N–H, C=O and N groups mean only these pairs line up, which is why the two strands are complementary.

questions.q: Cisplatin, \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_{3})_{2}Cl_{2}]}\), is an anticancer drug. How does it prevent DNA replication in cancer cells?

options.A: Its ammonia ligands form hydrogen bonds with the bases, holding the two strands together.
options.B: It breaks the phosphate–sugar bonds, splitting the DNA strand.
options.C: In a ligand replacement reaction, chloride ligands are replaced, and platinum forms a bond to a nitrogen atom on guanine, so the DNA strands cannot separate and copy correctly.
options.D: It replaces guanine in the DNA strand with a platinum atom.

questions.solution: Inside the cell the chloride ligands of cisplatin are replaced, and the platinum forms coordinate bonds to nitrogen atoms on guanine bases, often two neighbouring guanines. This distorts the DNA and stops it unwinding for replication, so the cell cannot divide. It also affects healthy cells, which causes side effects.
